You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

Visualize the entropy of a code base with a 3d force-directed graph.

The more decoupled and modular a code base is, the more spread and clustered the graph will look like.

Ensure your code base decoupling by creating your own rules and enforcing them with dep-tree check

## Supported languages
## Install On Mac and Linux, it can be installed using brew: ```shell brew install dep-tree ``` Alternatively, on any platform including Windows it can be installed with `pip`... ```shell pip install python-dep-tree ``` ...or `npm`: ```shell npm install @dep-tree/cli ``` ## About Dep Tree `dep-tree` is a cli tool for visualizing the complexity of a code base, and creating rules for ensuring its loosely coupling. It works with files, meaning that each file is a node in the dependency tree: - It starts from one or more entrypoints, which are usually the main executable files in a program or the files that expose the contents of a library (like `package/main.py`, `src/index.ts`, `src/lib.rs`...). - It makes a parent node out of the root file, and one child node for each imported file. > [!NOTE] > it only takes into account local files, not files imported from external libraries. - That process is repeated recursively with all the imported files, until the file dependency graph is formed. - If rendering the **code base entropy**, the nodes will be rendered using a 3d force-directed graph in the browser. - If rendering the **dependency tree** in the terminal, the nodes will be placed in a human-readable way, and users can navigate through the graph using the keyboard. - If validating the **dependency rules** in a CI system, it will check that the dependencies between files match some boundaries declared in a `.dep-tree.yml` file. ## Usage ### Entropy Choose the file that will act as the root of the dependency graph (for example `src/index.ts`), and run: ```shell dep-tree entropy src/index.ts ``` You can also pass multiple files if you don't have a single entrypoint: ```shell dep-tree entropy src/* ``` It will open a browser window and will render your file dependency graph using a 3d force-directed graph. The spheres (files) will be placed mimicking some attraction/repulsion forces. Some parts of your code base will tend to gravitate together if they are tightly coupled, and will tend to be separated if they are loosely coupled. The 3d graph for a clean code base will have groups of nodes clustered together and clearly separated from other clusters:
The 3d graph for a tightly coupled code base will have all the nodes grouped together with no clustering and no clear separation between them:

# Files that should be completely ignored by dep-tree. It's fine to ignore
# some big files that everyone depends on and that don't add
# value to the visualization, like auto generated code.
exclude:
  - 'some-glob-pattern/**/*.ts'

# The only files that will be included by dep-tree. If a file does not
# match any of the provided patters, it is ignored.
only:
  - 'some-glob-pattern/**/*.ts'

# Whether to unwrap re-exports to the target file or not.
# Imagine that you have the following setup:
#
#  src/index.ts     -> import { foo } from './foo'
#  src/foo/index.ts -> export { bar as foo } from './bar'
#  src/foo/bar.ts   -> export function bar() {}
#
# If `unwrapExports` is true, a dependency will be created from
# `src/index.ts` to `src/foo/bar.ts`, and the middle file `src/foo/index.ts`
# will be ignored, as it's just there for re-exporting the `bar` symbol,
# which is actually declared on `src/foo/bar.ts`
#
# If `unwrapExports` is false, re-exported symbols will not be traced back
# to where they are declared, and instead two dependencies will be created:
# - from `src/index.ts` to `src/foo/index.ts`
# - from `src/foo/index.ts` to `src/foo/bar.ts`
#
# Entropy visualization tends to lead to better results if this is set to `false`,
# but CLI rendering is slightly better with this set to `true`.
unwrapExports: false

# Check configuration for the `dep-tree check` command. Dep Tree will check for dependency
# violation rules declared here, and fail if there is at least one unsatisfied rule.
check:
  # These are the entrypoints to your application. Dependencies will be checked with
  # these files as root nodes. Typically, an application has only one entrypoint, which
  # is the executable file (`src/index.ts`, `main.py`, `src/lib.rs`, ...), but here
  # you can declare as many as you want.
  entrypoints:
    - src/index.ts

  # Whether to allow circular dependencies or not. Languages typically allow
  # having circular dependencies, but that has an impact in execution path
  # traceability, so you might want to disallow it.
  allowCircularDependencies: false

  # map from glob pattern to array of glob patterns that determines the exclusive allowed
  # dependencies that a file matching a key glob pattern might have. If file that
  # matches a key glob pattern depends on another file that does not match any of
  # the glob patterns declared in the values array, the check will fail.
  allow:
    # example: any file in `src/products` can only depend on files that are also
    # in the `src/products` folder or in the `src/helpers` folder.
    'src/products/**':
      - 'src/products/**'
      - 'src/helpers/**'
    # additionally, instead of providing a simple list of allowed dependencies, you
    # can also provide the reason for this restriction to exist, that way, when if the
    # check fails, an informative error is displayed through stderr.
    'src/users/**':

  # dependencies. If a file that matches a key glob pattern depends on another

from cyc import elementary_cycles
from collections import deque
cases=json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
def bfs(edges, entries):
    seen=[]
    for e in entries:
        if e in seen: continue
        q=deque([e]); seen.append(e)
        while q:
            x=q.popleft()
            for y in edges[x]:
                if y not in seen: seen.append(y); q.append(y)
    return seen
okset=0; okord=0
for c in cases:
    nodes=bfs(c['edges'], c['entries'])
    ids=c['ids']

    pred=['- '+' -> '.join(x+'.ts' for x in cy) for cy in cycles]
    lines=[l for l in c['err'].split('\n') if l.startswith('- ')]
    if set(pred)==set(lines): okset+=1
    else: print('SET MISMATCH', c['edges'], c['entries'], lines, pred)
    if pred==lines: okord+=1
    else: print('ORD', lines, pred)
print(okset, okord, len(cases))

func (lx *lexer) push(state stateFn) {
	lx.stack = append(lx.stack, state)

func (lx *lexer) pop() stateFn {
	if len(lx.stack) == 0 {
		panic("BUG in lexer: no states to pop")
	}
	last := lx.stack[len(lx.stack)-1]
	lx.stack = lx.stack[0 : len(lx.stack)-1]

func (lx *lexer) current() string {
	return lx.input[lx.start:lx.pos]

func (lx lexer) getPos() Position {
	p := Position{
		Line:  lx.line,
		Start: lx.start,
		Len:   lx.pos - lx.start,
	}
	if p.Len <= 0 {
		p.Len = 1
	}
	return p
}

func (lx *lexer) emit(typ itemType) {
	// Needed for multiline strings ending with an incomplete UTF-8 sequence.
	if lx.start > lx.pos {

		return

	lx.items <- item{typ: typ, pos: lx.getPos(), val: lx.current()}
	lx.start = lx.pos
}

func (lx *lexer) next() (r rune) {
	if lx.atEOF {

	if lx.pos >= len(lx.input) {

		lx.line++

	lx.prevWidths[2] = lx.prevWidths[1]

func (lx *lexer) backup() {
	if lx.atEOF {

	for {

func (lx *lexer) error(err error) stateFn {
	if lx.atEOF {
		return lx.errorPrevLine(err)
	}
	lx.items <- item{typ: itemError, pos: lx.getPos(), err: err}
	return nil
}

	pos := lx.getPos()
	pos.Line--
	pos.Len = 1
	pos.Start = lx.pos - 1
	lx.items <- item{typ: itemError, pos: pos, err: err}
	return nil

I've rebuilt dep-tree v0.23.4 in Go and committed it. On everything I compared against the original binary, the output matches. Running `./compile.sh` on a fresh clone builds `./executable` with no network access and no module cache needed, because all dependencies are vendored into the repo.

**What's in it:**
- **Commands:** the cobra CLI with the same help text, flags, aliases (`init`), version output and error messages. That includes the hidden way a bare file argument becomes `entropy`, and completion scripts that match the original's older cobra version.
- **Config:** strict `.dep-tree.yml` parsing that gives the same error messages, including Go type names like `config.Config` and `[]check.BlackListEntry`. `config` writes the same sample file, mode 0600.
- **JS/TS:** a token matcher that copies the original's quirks:
  - Imports come first, then re-exports, and re-exports override each other by name. `export *` takes its names from the target file.
  - Relative paths resolve with the same extension and index rules, and a folder's own `package.json` `main` is used.
  - npm workspaces and tsconfig `baseUrl`/`paths` behave the same, including their odd path substitution.
- **Python:** the same root files (`setup.py`, `pyproject.toml`, `requirements.txt`, `poetry.lock`), search order (file's folder, then root) and error messages.
- **Rust:** `Cargo.toml` roots and the module tree for `crate::`/`self::`/`super::`.
- **Go:** `go.mod` handling and dependencies on the specific file that declares each symbol used, via the standard Go parser.
- **Graph:** files load breadth-first, one entrypoint at a time. Cycle detection follows the original exactly for one entrypoint, and uses a different rule when there are several.
- **Outputs:**
  - `tree --json`, `check`, `explain` and the progress spinner on stderr.
  - `entropy` produces a byte-identical HTML file.
  - The interactive `tree` view, with the same drawing, colours and keys.

**Things that work differently from what you might expect:**
- **Inert settings:** `--unwrap-exports`, `--js-workspaces`, `--js-tsconfig-paths` and `--python-exclude-conditional-imports` (and the matching config keys) do nothing. They also do nothing in the original, so I copied that.
- **Faithful quirks:** several of the original's bugs are copied on purpose.
  - A Rust entrypoint with no `Cargo.toml`, or a `go.mod` with no module line, crashes with exit code 2.
  - `check` gives up on cycle detection after 3 seconds and then passes.
  - Without a terminal, `tree` fails with "exit status 1".
  - JS files with no named `package.json`, and Python files with no root file, get empty display names.
- **Copied from the original:** the large web-app part of the entropy HTML, and the bash/PowerShell completion scripts, are taken from the original's own output. There was no other way to get identical bytes.
- **Patched library:** the vendored TOML parser is patched so its error messages match the older version the original used.

**Testing:** I compared both binaries side by side using:
- hand-written cases for each language;
- random dependency graphs, for `tree`, `entropy` and `check`;
- random source files for the JS, Python and Rust parsers;
- 2,749 real JS/TS files and 327 Rust crates (outputs identical, apart from huge files where the original timed out);
- Python's standard library and the cobra Go module;
- about 400 terminal-view sessions driven through tmux.

**Differences that remain:**
- **Random ordering in the original:**
  - The order of cycles listed by `check` changes from run to run.
  - Which links are flagged as cyclic in `entropy` with several entrypoints also comes out in a varying order.
  - When two Go files in one package declare the same name, the file it picks varies between runs.
- **`check` cycle timeout:** my cycle search is faster, so on graphs with around a million cycles mine may finish inside the 3 seconds where the original times out.
- **Version-specific errors:** a few error messages for badly broken `Cargo.toml`, `tsconfig.json` or `go.mod` files may still differ slightly.

I've finished the Go reimplementation of dep-tree v0.23.4 and committed it. `./compile.sh` builds `./executable` from a fresh clone with no network or module cache needed, since all dependencies are committed under `vendor/`. On thousands of differential comparisons against the original binary, outputs match except where the original is itself random or slow.

**What was compared:** output, exit code and stderr (with the progress-bar timing numbers stripped) for each case:
- **CLI:** help text for every command, all four shell-completion scripts, and argument and config error messages.
- **JS/TS:** all 2,749 JS/TS files found on the system matched, plus random-snippet tests and synthetic projects.
- **Python:** a copied set of standard-library packages and random-snippet tests matched.
- **Rust:** 327 of 329 crates in the local cargo registry matched. The other two (`web-sys`, `winapi`) are huge, and the original didn't finish within the 20-second limit.
- **Go:** cobra and tcell from the module cache matched, apart from the duplicate-symbol case below.
- **`tree --json`, `check`, `explain`, entropy HTML:** randomly generated dependency graphs matched.
- **Interactive tree:** about 400 tmux sessions with key presses matched, including projects without a `package.json`.

**Known mismatches**, mostly cases where the original isn't consistent with itself:
- **Cycle order in `check`:** cycles that start at the same file come out in a random order from one run to the next; I use import order.
- **Duplicate cyclic links in multi-entrypoint entropy:** the original also orders these randomly.
- **Duplicate Go symbols** (e.g. files split by build tag, like `command_win.go` / `command_notwin.go`): the original picks either file at random; mine takes the last one alphabetically.
- **Map-ordered config:** when several `allow`/`deny` rules or tsconfig `paths` patterns match the same file, the original's choice is random; mine follows the order in the file.
- **`check`'s 3-second cycle timeout:** the original gives up looking for cycles after 3 seconds, prints a timeout line and passes. Mine enumerates faster, so a graph with around a million cycles that the original abandons can finish in mine and be printed instead (seen on a synthetic 1-million-cycle graph).
- **Crash cases:** a Rust entrypoint with no `Cargo.toml`, or a `go.mod` with no `module` line, crashes the original. I print a similar crash trace and exit with code 2, but the memory addresses in it differ.
- **Malformed `Cargo.toml` errors:** the toml library I vendored is newer than the original's, so I patched it; a few rare messages may still differ (for example, newer TOML date formats the old version rejected).

**Things in the repo you might not expect:**
- The entropy page's large JavaScript bundle was taken from the original's own HTML output and is embedded (gzipped).
- The bash and PowerShell completion scripts were also captured from the original, because the cobra version available locally (1.10.2) generates different ones from the 1.8.0 it was built with.

Several behaviours look like bugs in v0.23.4 but I reproduced them on purpose:
- The `--unwrap-exports`, `--js-workspaces`, `--js-tsconfig-paths` and `--python-exclude-conditional-imports` flags (and their config-file equivalents) have no effect.
- Files with no `package.json` or Python project file above them get empty names.
- `export *` is resolved through the target file's actual exports, so `export * from` a file that exports nothing creates no dependency.
- `check` reports file names relative to the config file's folder.
- `explain` ignores `--only`.
